embedded-system-design-using-arm--cpsr.title: CPSR bit map
rows: sticky saturation flag in DSP extensions
Thumb state when 1, ARMv5 and later
embedded-system-design-using-arm--cpsr.note: In user mode a write to CPSR is ignored, so only privileged code can change the mode and mask bits.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--user-m.title: processor modes and their banked registers
rows: privileged code that needs user registers
embedded-system-design-using-arm--user-m.note: Each mode has its own r13 and r14, so an exception can switch stacks without first saving the old stack pointer.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--vector.title: exception vector table
embedded-system-design-using-arm--vector.note: A slot is only four bytes, so it normally holds a branch to the handler rather than the handler itself.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--barrel.title: shift folded into the operand path
lines: MOV  r0, r1, LSL #2      ; r0 = r1 * 4
ADD  r2, r3, r3, LSL #3  ; r2 = r3 * 9
MOV  r4, r5, ASR #1      ; r4 = r5 / 2, sign preserved
RSB  r6, r7, r7, LSL #1  ; r6 = 2 * r7 - r7
embedded-system-design-using-arm--barrel.note: The shift happens before the ALU, so a multiply by a small constant costs no extra instruction or cycle.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--data-p.title: data processing with flags and a condition
lines: SUBS r2, r0, r1      ; r2 = r0 - r1, update N Z C V
ADDNE r2, r2, #1     ; add 1 only when Z = 0
MUL  r3, r0, r1      ; r3 = r0 * r1, flags unchanged
AND  r4, r0, #0xFF   ; keep the low byte
embedded-system-design-using-arm--data-p.note: The S suffix makes the flags a side effect of the operation; the NE suffix then predicates the next instruction on them.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--load-s.title: three load-store addressing forms
lines: LDR  r0, [r1]            ; r0 = mem[r1]
LDR  r2, [r1, #4]        ; r2 = mem[r1 + 4], r1 unchanged
LDR  r3, [r1, #8]!       ; pre-index: r1 += 8, then load
STR  r4, [r1], #-4       ; post-index: store, then r1 -= 4
embedded-system-design-using-arm--load-s.note: The exclamation mark writes the computed address back to the base register, which is how a loop walks an array.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--multip.title: callee-save prologue and epilogue
lines: func  STMFD sp!, {r4-r7, lr}   ; push 5 words, sp -= 20
MOV   r4, r0
BL    helper
ADD   r0, r0, r4
LDMFD sp!, {r4-r7, pc}   ; pop and return through pc
embedded-system-design-using-arm--multip.note: Restoring pc from the stack performs the return, so the epilogue needs no separate branch instruction.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--condit.title: condition suffixes and the flags they test
rows: signed greater or equal / less than
always, the default when no suffix is given
embedded-system-design-using-arm--condit.note: The condition occupies bits 31:28 of the instruction word, so almost every ARM instruction can be predicated.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--atpcs.title: register roles across an ATPCS call
rows: first four arguments, then the return value
embedded-system-design-using-arm--atpcs.note: Only r0 to r3 carry arguments, so a fifth argument is already pushed on the stack before the call.

embedded-system-design-using-arm--arm-th.title: switching state with BLX and BX
lines: CODE32
start BLX  thumb_inc      ; ARM to Thumb, T set from target bit 0
ADD  r2, r0, #1     ; back in ARM state
CODE16
thumb_inc
ADD  r0, #1         ; 16-bit Thumb encoding
BX   lr             ; return, state read from lr bit 0
embedded-system-design-using-arm--arm-th.note: Bit 0 of a code address selects the state, so BX and BLX change instruction set without a CPSR mode change.
